target: AG1's claim that AI's societal benefits outweigh its harms
objection: AI harms the economic well-being of many people and businesses, undermines critical thinking in students and adults, worsens racism by repeating and exacerbating bias against racial minorities, and poses dangerous privacy risks; on that basis, AI is not good for society overall.

target: AG2's claim that AI's harms are unavoidable and can only be reduced by perfect elimination
objection: The harms cited by the opponent—privacy risks, bias/racism, disruption of tasks, and misuse that weakens learning—are not inherent, unavoidable features of AI; they depend on data quality, system design, user incentives, oversight, and technical controls, so appropriate safeguards can substantially reduce or prevent them.

target: AG1's assumption that safeguards and governance can substantially reduce AI harms enough for benefits to dominate
objection: AI is commonly deployed under profit-and-scale incentives that encourage extensive data collection, aggressive targeting, and automation that shifts risks onto workers and the public, so privacy harms, economic harms, and other negative externalities remain likely in real-world deployment; safeguards generally cannot reliably prevent these harms at large scale.

target: AG2's claim that any remaining harms mean AI is not good for society
objection: A technology can be good for society based on net effects, not on eliminating every harm, so persistent residual harms do not by themselves show AI is not good overall; AI's benefits in health, accessibility, safety, and convenience can still outweigh residual risks.

target: AG1's claim that AI's benefits are not undermined by critical-thinking concerns
objection: AI often gives ready-made answers, summaries, and recommendations that people rely on without fully evaluating evidence, which weakens critical thinking; because health, education, and work benefits depend on good reasoning, degraded critical thinking undermines the reliability of those benefits and thus AI is not good overall.

target: AG2's claim that AI necessarily weakens critical thinking and therefore undermines its benefits
objection: AI can be configured to support critical thinking by showing sources, highlighting uncertainty, prompting diagnostic questions, and giving feedback or corrections, so AI use can strengthen rather than weaken users' reasoning; therefore the claimed benefits in health, education, and work are not inherently undermined by AI-supported convenience.

target: AG2's claim that lower end-user critical thinking inherently defeats AI safety and accessibility benefits
objection: Safety monitoring and accessibility tools do not all depend on ordinary users scrutinizing AI reasoning; workplace-safety systems can operate as automated prevention layers and accessibility tools can directly enable communication and participation, so weaker critical thinking does not inherently eliminate those benefits.

target: AG1's claim that safety and accessibility benefits survive even if users rely on AI outputs
objection: Workplace-safety outputs and accessibility outputs still require users to interpret them, and critical-thinking decline makes people more likely to misread safety alerts or miss accessibility errors; those harms are therefore tied to the exact benefit channels AG1 relies on, not just to schoolwork or abstract reasoning.

target: AG2's claim that critical-thinking decline makes AI safety and accessibility outputs unreliable in practice
objection: Safety-critical AI can be embedded in structured safety procedures with fail-safes and interlocks, and accessibility tools often include review and correction interfaces, so lower personal critical thinking does not inherently produce harmful misinterpretations or uncorrected errors.

target: AG1's claim that institutional oversight and correction loops make safety/accessibility AI reliably operative
objection: Even with nominal oversight, workers and caretakers often defer to AI due to automation bias and time pressure, and correction loops such as auditing and rollback are costly and constrained, so errors can persist long enough to cause harm before being fixed.

target: AG2's claim that correction loops cannot reliably preserve AI safety/accessibility benefits at scale
objection: Safety-critical and care-critical deployments can use logging, monitoring, auditing, updates, and rollback procedures, making correction loops reasonably reliable at real-world scale; with those loops, the main benefit pathways for accident prevention and participation support can remain operative.

target: AG1's claim that correction loops can catch and correct AI failures reliably enough
objection: The most dangerous failures are often rare, so incident logs and audits may not capture enough representative cases, and distribution shifts can cause corrected errors to reappear in new settings; therefore correction loops cannot be assumed to reliably preserve safety and accessibility benefits.

target: AG2's claim that rare failures and distribution shift make AI benefit pathways unreliable
objection: Organizations can instrument AI systems to log outputs, detect anomalies, support auditing, and roll back updates, so correction loops can function with reasonable reliability; that means safety and accessibility benefit pathways can remain operative despite some user over-reliance.

target: AG1's claim that correction loops and monitoring can reliably maintain safety/accessibility benefits
objection: In real-world high-stakes settings, logs and audits may miss rare, high-impact failures, and distribution shift can cause previously fixed errors to reappear after updates; therefore the claimed safety and accessibility benefit pathways are not reliably operative in practice.

target: AG2's economic-harm argument against AI
objection: AI can improve economic well-being by automating routine work, boosting productivity, lowering barriers for small businesses through low-marginal-cost software services, and increasing participation for people with disabilities, so AI need not mainly harm workers or small businesses and can be net positive economically.

target: AG1's claim that economic, safety, and accessibility benefits outweigh harms
objection: AI safety and accessibility functions require collecting, analyzing, and storing sensitive personal data such as voice, images, location, work behavior, or health-related information; at scale those privacy risks can deter participation and impose harms, undermining the real-world value of those benefits.

target: AG2's claim that privacy risks are intrinsic to AI safety/accessibility benefits
objection: Accessibility and safety functions do not inherently require unsafe long-term collection of sensitive data; they can be built with privacy-preserving practices like minimization, encryption, limited retention, and on-device processing, making privacy risk a deployment choice rather than an unavoidable property of the benefits.

target: AG1's claim that privacy-preserving design can eliminate privacy harms enough to preserve benefits
objection: Privacy-preserving methods do not fully eliminate privacy harms, because models can still infer sensitive traits or leak memorized information; if those harms persist, they can still deter participation and reduce the real-world value of safety and accessibility tools.

target: AG2's claim that inference and memorization make privacy harms unavoidable at damaging levels
objection: Privacy-preserving machine-learning methods and deployment controls can substantially reduce leakage and prevent meaningful re-identification, so privacy harms from inference and memorization are real but not inevitable at damaging levels.

target: AG1's claim that privacy-preserving methods sufficiently constrain privacy risk
objection: Privacy-preserving techniques provide only probabilistic and bounded protection, not absolute guarantees, especially against auxiliary data and repeated queries; residual privacy harms can still occur at damaging levels and deter participation in safety and accessibility tools.

target: AG2's claim that even privacy-preserving controls cannot sufficiently reduce privacy harms
objection: Differential privacy can provide formal, quantifiable bounds on inference risk, and with privacy budgets, user controls, and consent, residual risk is unlikely to deter participation enough to negate the practical value of safety and accessibility tools.

target: AG1's claim that strict privacy protections can preserve both reliability and benefits
objection: Strong privacy protections usually require heavy minimization, noise, restricted access, and auditing, which reduce available signal and increase operational friction; in safety- and accessibility-critical uses those constraints can lower output reliability and also worsen economic harms by favoring large vendors and consolidating adoption.

target: AG2's claim that strong privacy protections necessarily undermine AI usefulness
objection: Privacy-preserving approaches can still retain enough task-relevant signal for accurate accessibility and safety outputs, and any added operational friction need not eliminate the core functions of hazard prevention and disability accessibility, so privacy safeguards do not inherently make AI net harmful.

target: AG1's claim that privacy-preserving design can avoid unacceptable reliability loss
objection: Strict privacy-preserving measures inherently reduce usable signal or add uncertainty, which increases error and false-positive/false-negative rates; in safety-critical and participation-critical contexts even modest reliability losses can create accidents or exclusion, so privacy-preserving design undermines the core benefit pathways.

target: AG2's claim that privacy constraints make safety/accessibility thresholds impossible to meet
objection: Safety and accessibility deployments are judged against task-specific reliability requirements, and privacy-preserving methods can be tuned to satisfy those thresholds; with monitoring, escalation, and fallback procedures, residual uncertainty need not produce widespread harm.

target: AG1's claim that privacy-preserving evaluation can certify reliability well enough
objection: Privacy-preserving evaluation and limited logging can hide subgroup and edge-case failures, making it impossible to reliably validate whether outputs meet safety or accessibility thresholds across real users and contexts; as a result, threshold-miss errors can still cause accidents or exclusion at scale.

target: AG2's claim that privacy-constrained evaluation cannot support reliable deployment
objection: Teams can use privacy-preserving evaluation datasets, aggregate telemetry, secure-enclave evaluation, offline testing, and human-in-the-loop audits to estimate performance without unlimited access to raw sensitive inputs, allowing them to certify reliability sufficiently for safety and accessibility deployments.

target: AG1's claim that privacy-preserving evaluation can reliably validate thresholds across real populations
objection: Task thresholds in safety and accessibility depend on rare failure modes and subgroup-specific performance, and privacy-preserving evaluation often removes the fine-grained signals needed to diagnose those cases; therefore privacy-constrained certification cannot reliably validate real-world reliability and can still produce safety/accessibility harms.
